extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the USPTO 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (and July 2015 examples) to analyze patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B framework, including when to issue rejections or reasons for allowance and how to phrase Office action remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are analyzed for eligibility in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims in the examples are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation; fact patterns should be interpreted based on the set forth examples, but other fact patterns may have different eligibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites one of the statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a series of acts it is a process; if it recites a device or set of devices it may be a machine; a non‑transitory computer‑readable medium is a manufacture. Establishing Step 1 (YES) is the first step in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claim elements recite abstract ideas such as organizing/comparing information, mathematical algorithms, mental processes, or laws of nature. Provide specific comparison to precedent (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene, Benson, Flook, Grams, etc.) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types/examples of abstract ideas and judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize categories of judicial exceptions: mental processes, mathematical concepts/algorithms, and other basic concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the guidance treat 'comparing and formatting information' as a mental process, 'calculating a scaling factor' as a mathematical algorithm, and equations (e.g., Arrhenius) as laws of nature/mathematical relationships. Use case law analogies to classify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Significantly more analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, determine whether additional elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether additional limitations provide meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the abstract idea to a technological environment. Evaluate both individual elements and the claimed ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of generic computer components performing generic functions does not, by itself, amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑level recitations of a microprocessor, memory, transmitter, database, user interface, etc., performing conventional functions (receiving, processing, transmitting, displaying) are 'well‑understood, routine and conventional' and do not provide meaningful limitations (examples: meal planner, stock quote filtering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field‑of‑use / technological environment limitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., the Internet, GUI) does not by itself make the claim significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet limitations are merely a field of use; merely linking the idea to the Internet or other environment does not transform an abstract idea into patent‑eligible subject matter (e.g., claims that simply use the Internet to implement an organizing/comparing idea remain ineligible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination can provide significantly more (technologically rooted solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered combination of otherwise conventional elements may, together, provide meaningful limitations amounting to significantly more, particularly when the combination solves a technological problem rooted in computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transmitting an alert via wireless channel to activate an application and enable later connection when the subscriber's computer comes online constitutes a technologically‑rooted solution (DDR Holdings analogy) and can be eligible when taken as an ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble and claim limitation effect (MPEP 2111.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether preamble language merely states purpose/field of use or actually limits claim scope; a non‑limiting preamble does not add 'life, meaning and vitality' to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preamble only states purpose/field of use it ordinarily does not limit the claim; do not treat a non‑limiting preamble as an additional limitation in Step 2B (see example of GUI meal planning preamble).

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Computer‑implemented’/‘apply it’ limitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply adding 'computer‑implemented' or similar language is akin to saying 'apply it' and is not enough to amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent shows that merely requiring that an abstract idea be implemented on a computer or in a particular technological environment does not transform it into significantly more (see Flook and related examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that improve computer technology or another technical field support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that provides an improvement in computer technology or another technical field, or transforms matter, can be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: GUI relocating obscured text that is necessarily rooted in computer technology; software that controls a rubber molding press to improve precision molding (transforms material/state); internal combustion engine control that improves engine technology. Improvements must be integrated and provide meaningful limitations, not mere field‑of‑use labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical algorithms and laws of nature require special care
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical procedures and equations (e.g., scaling factor algorithms, Arrhenius equation) are likely abstract and require Step 2B scrutiny whether additional claimed elements amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mathematical relationship is recited, determine whether additional elements integrate the math into a control scheme or otherwise improve technology (e.g., automated control of press), thereby providing significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑transitory computer‑readable medium claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting 'non‑transitory' ensures the claim does not encompass transitory signals and asserts a manufacture category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this language when the claim is for stored instructions; recognizing 'non‑transitory' helps clarify statutory category and exclude signal‑based subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis for clearly eligible claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self‑evident (e.g., claim clearly amounts to significantly more or is not directed to any exception), a streamlined analysis can be used and a written rejection need not be issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims like certain engine or BIOS examples where the claim as a whole clearly provides significant meaningful limitations, examiners may conclude eligibility without performing full Steps 2A/2B and may add clarifying remarks if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection content guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection under §101, identify the judicial exception and explain why the claim recites it by pointing to specific claim steps; also explain why additional elements do not add significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: point to filtering/generating/formatting steps as mental processes or to generating/scaling steps as mathematical algorithms; explain why transmission server/microprocessor/memory are only generic computer functions and do not impose meaningful limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remarks for allowance / reasons for allowance guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is allowed but recites an exception in part, add remarks or reasons for allowance clarifying that while the claim recites an abstract idea or other exception, additional limitations amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include language identifying the abstract idea and indicating which additional limitations (as ordered combination) provide a technologically‑rooted solution or meaningful limits (e.g., activation via wireless device enabling later Internet connection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent to frame analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply and analogize to relevant court decisions (e.g., Cyberfone, SmartGene, DDR Holdings, Flook, Benson, Grams) to characterize the exception and the sufficiency of additional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples repeatedly map claim features to prior judicial characterizations: organizing/comparing information (mental processes), mathematical conversions/algorithms (Benson/Flook), and technology‑rooted solutions (DDR Holdings). Use such analogies to support Step 2A/2B conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High‑level claim language construed broadly weakens the showing of significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements recited at a high level of generality will be construed broadly as generic and thus less likely to supply meaningful limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim does not expressly recite how components perform unconventional functions, the examiner should construe them at the highest reasonable level of generality and treat them as generic (examples: 'user interface', 'database', 'transmission server').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination vs individual element analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate additional claim elements both individually and as an ordered combination for whether they amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual limitations are routine, their particular combination may be unconventional and solve a technical problem (compare ineligible Claim 1 vs eligible Claim 2 in the stock quote example). Document the reasoning for both perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document factual bases when relying on conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: If concluding that elements are well‑understood, routine, and conventional, the examiner should articulate why (and identify which elements) to support the Step 2B conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples instruct examiners to explain that components only perform basic functions (e.g., storing information, displaying output, accepting input) and therefore are not meaningfully limiting; include such explanations in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that transform matter or improve manufacturing processes are likely eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes or claims that transform a physical material or improve a manufacturing process can provide significantly more than judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the precision rubber molding example: integrating a mathematical relationship into a control scheme that changes the state of material (curing rubber) and controls machinery can amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: When additional limitations merely automate human tasks, likely ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely automate tasks that can be performed mentally or by pen-and-paper (e.g., meal planning, selecting meals to meet goals) are typically directed to abstract ideas and lack significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples where the core concept is a mental process or organizing/comparing data; if the claimed computerization only provides automation without unconventional steps, reject under §101.
